prompt: Patients' records leak from a clinic because of a fault in a layer the provider runs. Who answers to the patients under the LGPD?
hint: The responsibility is split; are the consequences?

choices.text: The provider, because the fault was below the line
choices.why: The contract may say who pays whom; the patients' relationship is with the clinic, and the consequences stay with it.

choices.text: The clinic
choices.why: Right. The responsibility is split, the consequences are not.

choices.text: Nobody, since a shared responsibility is nobody's in particular
choices.why: Sharing the work does not dissolve the duty to the people whose data it is.

choices.text: The auditor who certified the provider's controls
choices.why: An auditor attests to a provider; it answers to nobody's patients.

prompt: Why is a third-party attestation the only evidence you can have for the rows below the line?
hint: What would you have to do to test them yourself?

choices.text: Because the provider's controls are secret by law
choices.why: No law makes them secret; you simply have no access to them.

choices.text: Because you cannot inspect them: no access to the hypervisor, the building or its staff's logs
choices.why: Right. So you read what an auditor who could inspect them wrote.

choices.text: Because an API request would cost money for each of them
choices.why: There is no API for them at any price; the provider's half is not settings in your account.

choices.text: Tests are less reliable than reports
choices.why: The opposite: a report is the weaker kind of evidence, used because it is the only one available.

prompt: Which of these are true of evidence collected through the API about your half? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare it with an auditor's report.

choices.text: It is specific to your account
choices.why: Right. No report covers one of your buckets.

choices.text: It describes the moment you asked
choices.why: Right. A setting read today is the setting today.

choices.text: It is the same for every customer of the provider
choices.why: That is the report's property, not the API's.

choices.text: Somebody at the provider collects it for you each quarter
choices.why: Nobody else will ask those questions about your account; that is the duty half of it.

prompt: Against moto, `get-bucket-encryption` on the new bucket answered `ServerSideEncryptionConfigurationNotFoundError`. What does that error mean?
hint: Three errors and one silence, and none of them a fault.

choices.text: The bucket does not exist
choices.why: It existed: `create-bucket` had just answered `/clinic-records`.

choices.text: Encryption is not available in São Paulo
choices.why: The same request set it a moment later, in the same region.

choices.text: Nobody has decided it yet
choices.why: Right. The API is saying no default encryption has been set on this bucket.

choices.text: The key `test` has no permission to read encryption settings
choices.why: Checking was off in this lesson, and a refusal would have said AccessDenied.

prompt: Match each bucket setting to what it decides.
hint: The table of four.

pairs.right: whether objects are encrypted at rest on arrival
whether a policy or an ACL can make it public
whether ACLs are in play at all
whether a deleted object can be brought back

right_distractors: which region the bucket lives in

prompt: Since April 2023, AWS creates new buckets with Block Public Access on. A bucket the clinic created in 2021 is checked today. What does that change tell you about it?
hint: When does a default apply?

choices.text: That it is protected too, since AWS changed the default for every bucket
choices.why: That change reached only buckets created after it; the old ones kept their settings.

choices.text: Nothing: it kept whatever it had, and only reading it back will tell
choices.why: Right. A default protects the buckets nobody thought about; an inventory finds the rest.

choices.text: That it was made public, since old buckets were public by default
choices.why: Old buckets were private by default too; the 403 in lesson 1 is that default. They simply lacked the guardrail.

choices.text: That AWS will refuse to serve it until somebody accepts the new defaults
choices.why: Nothing about old buckets stopped working; that is why they are easy to forget.

prompt: moto now reports all four Block Public Access switches on for `clinic-records`. Is that transcript proof that the bucket cannot be made public?
hint: Stored is not the same as enforced.

choices.text: Yes, because the setting was read back from the system that enforces it
choices.why: moto stores Block Public Access and enforces none of it; the reading is only as good as the system answering.

choices.text: No: this lab keeps those settings without applying them; AWS would apply them
choices.why: Right. The same reading from AWS would be evidence; from moto it is a stored value.

choices.text: No, because a read never proves anything; only a written policy does
choices.why: Reading back is exactly the evidence the lesson asks for; the problem is this particular system.

choices.text: Yes, as long as versioning is also enabled
choices.why: Versioning protects against deletion; it says nothing about who can read.

prompt: Of the four questions asked of the new bucket in moto, how many came back as an error message?
hint: One of them printed nothing.

prompt: Which report should a security engineer read to learn what a provider's controls did over the last year, and what failed?
hint: A certificate says a system exists.

choices.text: The SOC 3
choices.why: A short public summary with none of the detail; it does not list exceptions.

choices.text: The ISO/IEC 27001 certificate
choices.why: It certifies that a management system exists; it is not a list of tested controls and their results.

choices.text: The SOC 2 Type II
choices.why: Right. Named controls, tested over months, with the exceptions listed.

choices.text: The provider's own security whitepaper, which it publishes on its website for every customer
choices.why: Written by the provider about itself; an attestation is somebody independent testing it.

prompt: What are the complementary user entity controls in a SOC 2 report?
hint: The line, in an auditor's language.

choices.text: Controls the auditor recommends the provider add next year
choices.why: They are not recommendations to the provider; they are assumptions about the customer.

choices.text: Controls the provider assumes its customers operate
choices.why: Right. The report passed on the assumption that you do them.

choices.text: Controls that failed testing and were fixed during the audit period
choices.why: Those are exceptions, with the provider's answer beside them.

choices.text: Extra controls a customer can buy from the provider
choices.why: Nothing is for sale in that list; it is what you are expected to do yourself.

prompt: A SOC 2 Type II of a provider passed with no exceptions. Which questions does it leave unanswered? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does a report describe, and when?

choices.text: Whether one of your buckets is public
choices.why: Right. Nothing in your account is in the report.

choices.text: Whether a service outside its scope was examined
choices.why: Right. Outside the scope means not examined.

choices.text: Whether a change made after the period still holds
choices.why: Right. The report describes the past period only.

choices.text: Whether the tested controls worked during the period
choices.why: That is exactly the question it answers.

prompt: Where does AWS keep its compliance reports for customers?
hint: A portal in the console.

choices.text: AWS Artifact
choices.why: Right. Microsoft's equivalent is the Service Trust Portal, Google Cloud's Compliance Reports Manager.

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail, under the compliance tab
choices.why: CloudTrail records your account's API calls; lesson 15.

choices.text: A public page on the provider's website, with all reports open
choices.why: Some are public; most need an account and some an NDA.

choices.text: The Service Trust Portal
choices.why: That is Microsoft's.

prompt: How does the lesson treat Gartner's figure that 99% of cloud security failures would be the customer's fault?
hint: Was it counted?

choices.text: As a measured count of incidents through 2025
choices.why: It was a prediction made in 2019, and nobody published the tally.

choices.text: As a forecast whose direction holds up
choices.why: Right. An opinion from people who see many incidents.

choices.text: As marketing, and so to be ignored
choices.why: The lesson keeps the direction, because the incidents in the news fit it.

choices.text: As proof that providers never fail
choices.why: The same section describes a provider failing, in 2023.

prompt: In the Capital One incident of 2019, which half of the line did the failures sit in?
hint: A firewall the bank ran, and a role the bank wrote.

choices.text: The provider's: AWS's storage service leaked the data because of a fault in its own access checks
choices.why: Storage did what the role's permissions allowed; the permissions were the bank's.

choices.text: Both, equally
choices.why: The provider's half did what it promised throughout.

choices.text: The customer's: a misconfigured firewall and a role allowed far more than it needed
choices.why: Right. Two of the bank's own settings combined.

choices.text: Neither: it was a zero-day in the hypervisor
choices.why: Nothing in the public account of it involves the hypervisor.

prompt: In the 2023 case, a stolen signing key let an intruder read mail in Exchange Online. What could a customer have done about a failure like that?
hint: It was below the line; what found it was above.

choices.text: Prevented it, by rotating the signing key every month
choices.why: The signing key was the provider's; no customer could rotate it.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since it was the provider's half
choices.why: One customer did something: it noticed, in its own audit records, and reported it.

choices.text: Detected it, in audit records it chose to collect
choices.why: Right. That is how the US State Department found it.

choices.text: Avoided it by keeping the mail encrypted at rest
choices.why: The forged tokens were accepted as the users themselves; encryption at rest does not refuse an authorised reader. Lesson 11.

prompt: Match each failure to the row of the stack it sits in.
hint: The table of the section.

pairs.right: data, and who can reach it

pairs.left: a key in a repository, still valid
a rule open to the world on an administrative port

prompt: Under shared fate, AWS made Block Public Access the default for new buckets. Whose row is public access now?
hint: A default is a setting in your account.

choices.text: The provider's, since it now decides it
choices.why: It decides a starting point; you can change it in one request, and the consequences stay yours.

choices.text: Still the customer's
choices.why: Right. The line has not moved in any contract; the work in the row has been started for you.

choices.text: Shared equally between the two, under a new contract
choices.why: No new contract came with the default.

choices.text: The auditor's, who checks the default each year
choices.why: An auditor of the provider never looks at your buckets.

prompt: Match each kind of help to an example.
hint: Default, guardrail, blueprint.

pairs.right: Block Public Access on for new buckets
an organisation policy denying regions outside Brazil
a tested landing zone of accounts, networks and logs

right_distractors: an auditor's report on the provider

prompt: caio switches a guardrail off on a test bucket to make an upload from a partner's system work. What does the lesson ask of that?
hint: Keep the defaults.

choices.text: Nothing, since test buckets are outside the line
choices.why: A test bucket is a bucket in your account like any other.

choices.text: That AWS approve the change first
choices.why: There is no approval step; the API does what a valid key asks.

choices.text: Treat it as a decision with a written reason, and know it is a resource the default no longer covers
choices.why: Right. Every public bucket of lesson 9 began as somebody turning a guardrail off to make something work.

choices.text: Undo it at once, because a guardrail may never be switched off
choices.why: The lesson asks for a written reason, not a ban; sometimes there is a good one.

prompt: AWS says it is responsible for the security ___ the cloud, and the customer for the security in it.
hint: A two-letter word in English.

prompt: Put the steps of section 03 in the order they ran.
hint: Ask, decide, ask again.
items: ask for the four settings and get three errors and a silence
set encryption, public access, ownership and versioning
ask for the four settings again and keep the answers
trap: Ending after the writes is the slip: they printed nothing, and only the second reading is evidence.

prompt: An auditor asks the clinic for evidence that patient records are encrypted at rest. Which pair answers both halves of the line?
hint: One piece for what you cannot see, one for what you can.

choices.text: The provider's SOC 2 Type II, and a transcript reading the bucket's encryption back
choices.why: Right. The report for the provider's storage and keys, the API for your setting.

choices.text: Two transcripts, one per half
choices.why: There is no API for the provider's half; you cannot produce a transcript of it.

choices.text: The provider's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate on its own
choices.why: It says nothing about your bucket, and the line leaves your setting to you.

choices.text: A screenshot of the AWS announcement saying that encryption has been on by default for every new object since 2023
choices.why: A default is a starting point; it says nothing about what this bucket does today.
